parts.title: Linguistic Diversity
parts.article:
(A) More than half of the world's languages are at risk, but an unlikely saviour is at hand. What is an endangered language? As a rough guide, any language with fewer than 10,000 speakers is in danger. However, the total number of speakers is not always a clear indication of the health of a language. In the South Andaman Islands, for example, fewer than 100 people speak Onge, but it is the primary language of those who do, and, critically, the first language of all the islands' children. Consequently, it would be considered less threatened than a language such as Chipewyan in Canada, where more than 4,000 belong to the ethnic group that uses the language, but there is little use among the new generation.

(B) It could be argued that in today's globalised world, we would be better off all speaking the same language, be it Chinese, English or Spanish. It might bring us closer together, and we would certainly be more likely to make our ideas comprehensible. The majority of linguists argue, however, that when it comes to language, diversity matters.

(C) “People's understanding of themselves, and their relationship with their environment are all framed in terms of concepts expressed in their own languages,” says Marcus Colchester, director of the Forest Peoples Programme. “Many indigenous peoples derive their identities from the way they live off their land. Day-to-day activities such as hunting, fishing and farming are directly connected to the spirits and mythic beings whose stories make these people who they are.”

(D) Louisa Maffi of Terralingua, an organisation that protects cultural and biological diversity, believes linguistic diversity is of immense value to humanity as a whole. As we lose each language, we lose a repository of knowledge, values and beliefs that, in many cases, provide alternative solutions to human problems; we diminish that pool of creativity and inventiveness, and our ability to adapt to changing circumstances.

(E) Nicholas Ostler, chairman of the Foundation for Endangered Languages, points out the scientific interest in maintaining linguistic diversity. To lose diversity will mean losing awareness of the many and varied features of human language — what part of our vocal tract we use for communication, the different ways we use words to reflect meaning, and so on.

(F) Historically, colonial governments practised policies of compelling minority cultures to speak the majority language. But even where there was little or no forced assimilation, imperialism still took its toll. Ostler cites the example of the ancient Roman Empire, which had no specific policy of forcing subjects to speak Latin, but still greatly reduced linguistic diversity across Europe. There was some prestige associated with the language—it was the medium of trade and administration—and people who wanted to get on in life tended to learn it. And similar processes are threatening minority languages today, says Ostler. “The Romans succeeded in making people live in larger communities, what we now call urbanisation. And nowadays people move from the countryside to cities where regional languages aren't maintained. The new generation grows up with their lives focused on the wider community. It may take several generations for the traditional language to fall out of use completely.”

(G) “Many nation states see cultural diversity as a threat to national unity,” says Maffi, “so monolingualism is promoted in specific contexts, particularly schools, where there is no multilingual education offered, and in government, where politics is only conducted in the national language. Such implicit endorsement of monolingualism conspires to place pressure on minority peoples to assimilate. There is essentially a misconceived either/or ideology: either you maintain your mother tongue, in which case you can't participate in national life, or you forget your mother tongue and learn the majority language.”

(H) In recent decades, the mass media have reinforced this process further and extended the penetration of metropolitan languages like English and Spanish beyond urban centres into smaller communities. The pervasive influence of the media has effectively created a cultural divide between the generations. Ostler continues, where young people speak their traditional language with their elders, but English among themselves. Maffi describes similar trends among indigenous minority groups worldwide. “All of the images children see in the media are of the glamorised lifestyle of the majority, and that lifestyle is communicated in the majority language. So it becomes very difficult for them to find a reason to value their own language.”

(I) When the internet first took off during the mid-1990s, many feared it represented the end of the road for endangered languages. Because it was only available to English-speakers, it would only serve to continue the decline. However, these fears proved to be unfounded, as the diversity of languages on the web increased rapidly in the years that followed. Peter Austin, of London's School of Oriental and African Studies, attributes this to the lack of control on the internet. “Unlike most TV or radio, the web isn't in the hands of big media corporations. All you need is an internet account and a little technology, and you can produce information, news, videos, and so on, as much as you want.” Minority groups around the world—in Hawaii, Mexico, Siberia, and many other places—are now taking advantage of this autonomy to document their language in written, audio and visual format. And, crucially, it is in a form which appeals to young people. It seems that the mass media could, after all, be the salvation of the world's most threatened languages.
parts.questions:
Questions 27–31
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 27–31 on your answer sheet, write:

Q27 The Onge language has a particularly poor chance of survival.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q28 Most linguists oppose the idea of a single global language.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q29 Many citizens of the Roman Empire chose to become Latin speakers.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q30 Majority languages such as Spanish and English are now spreading faster within smaller communities than larger ones.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q31 There is a greater proportion of English used on the internet nowadays than in the 1990s.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 32–35
Complete the summary using the list of words, A-I, below. Write the correct letter, A-I, in boxes 32–35 on your answer sheet.
Disappearing languages in today's globalised world
If everybody spoke the same language, whether Spanish, English or Chinese, there would certainly be less chance of between people. But would society suffer if there were one global language? Experts agree that it would.
According to Marcus Colchester, people's use of native languages is key to how they relate to their . He also emphasises the link between indigenous people's traditional and the recounting of the myths and folk tales which are integral to their sense of identity.
Louisa Maffi describes how loss of language diversity leads to a loss of collective human knowledge, so there could be fewer available to help solve problems in the world.
  • A ideas
  • B speakers
  • C connections
  • D surroundings
  • E families
  • F occupations
  • G relationship
  • H words
  • I misunderstandings
Questions 36–40
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 36–40 on your answer sheet.

Q36 In the first paragraph, the writer mentions two particular languages in order to indicate

  • A a key factor in determining how endangered a language is.
  • B alternative methods of interpreting data about languages at risk.
  • C different reasons why a minority language might be under threat.
  • D difficulties involved in assessing a language's survival prospects.

Q37 What similarity between the Roman Empire and the present day does Nicholas Ostler mention?

  • A the growth of international trade
  • B the shift towards living in more extended social groups
  • C the attitude of governments towards minority languages
  • D the speed with which minority languages fall out of use

Q38 According to Louisa Maffi, many people wrongly believe that

  • A it is more difficult for minority-language speakers to access education.
  • B majority-language speakers can participate better in national life.
  • C their national government is opposed to the use of minority languages.
  • D they need to choose between being a minority- or majority-language speaker.

Q39 What problem among minority-language speakers is mentioned in the eighth paragraph?

  • A younger people's perceptions of their mother tongue
  • B breakdown of communication between the generations
  • C older people's attitudes to their children's language use
  • D generational differences in ability to access the mass media

Q40 What does Peter Austin see as the main advantage of the internet for minority language groups?

  • A the variety of media it can use
  • B the freedom its users can have
  • C the wide geographical area it can reach
  • D the range of people it can be accessed by

reference:
Q27

解析 原文明确表示Onge语因为是岛上所有孩子的第一语言，所以被认为受到威胁较小（less threatened），这与题目中所说的“存活几率极低（poor chance of survival）”截然相反。

干扰 你可能只看到不到100人使用这门语言就觉得它快灭绝了，但别漏了后半句“它是孩子们的第一语言”，这说明它具有生命力。

句子 In the South Andaman Islands, for example, fewer than 100 people speak Onge, but it is the primary language of those who do, and, critically, the first language of all the islands' children. Consequently, it would be considered less threatened than a language such as Chipewyan in Canada, where more than 4,000 belong to the ethnic group that uses the language, but there is little use among the new generation.

Q28

解析 原文明确指出大多数语言学家认为语言的多样性至关重要（diversity matters），这在逻辑上直接等同于他们反对只存在单一的全球语言。

干扰 你可能觉得原文没有直接出现“oppose”这个词，但是“认为多样性很重要”在语义上直接证明了对单一化（single global language）的反对。

句子 The majority of linguists argue, however, that when it comes to language, diversity matters.

Q29

解析 原文提到罗马帝国没有强迫人们说拉丁语，而是人们为了个人发展主动去学习它（tended to learn it），这与题目中的“选择成为（chose to become）”完全一致。

干扰 遇到历史类的题目你可能会过度推测，但只要抓住“tended to learn it”代表了民众的自主意愿，就能笃定选YES。

句子 Ostler cites the example of the ancient Roman Empire, which had no specific policy of forcing subjects to speak Latin, but still greatly reduced linguistic diversity across Europe. There was some prestige associated with the language—it was the medium of trade and administration—and people who wanted to get on in life tended to learn it.

Q30

解析 原文确实提到了英语和西班牙语等主流语言正在向更小的社区渗透，但根本没有把小社区和大型社区的“传播速度（spreading faster）”进行过任何对比。

干扰 看到原文同时出现了English, Spanish和smaller communities，你可能很容易脑补出它们在小社区传播得更快，但只要原文没做比较，出现比较级就是NOT GIVEN。

句子 In recent decades, the mass media have reinforced this process further and extended the penetration of metropolitan languages like English and Spanish beyond urban centres into smaller communities.

Q31

解析 原文提到90年代中期互联网只对英语使用者开放，但后来网上的语言多样性迅速增加，这意味着现在其他语言冲淡了英语的占比，英语的比例实际上变小了，而不是题目所说的“比例更大（greater proportion）”。

干扰 你可能以为随着互联网发展，英语在网上的绝对数量变多，其比例就会变大；但原文强调的是后来“语言多样性增加了”，这直接反驳了英语占比扩大的说法。

句子 When the internet first took off during the mid-1990s, many feared it represented the end of the road for endangered languages. Because it was only available to English-speakers, it would only serve to continue the decline. However, these fears proved to be unfounded, as the diversity of languages on the web increased rapidly in the years that followed.

Q32

解析 原文提到大家都说同样的语言会让我们的想法“更容易被理解（make our ideas comprehensible）”，这就对应了题目的减少人与人之间的“误解（misunderstandings）”。

干扰 你可能会直接把A选项（ideas）填进去，但原文是说“更容易理解彼此的想法”，逻辑上等于“更少的误解”，填ideas语法和含义都不通。

句子 It could be argued that in today's globalised world, we would be better off all speaking the same language, be it Chinese, English or Spanish. It might bring us closer together, and we would certainly be more likely to make our ideas comprehensible.

Q33

解析 原文里Marcus明确表示人们与“环境（environment）”的关系是通过他们自己的语言中的概念来构建的，environment完美替换为选项中的“周围环境（surroundings）”。

干扰 这道题的定位非常简单，你只需要抓准名词“environment”的同义替换，别被长难句绕晕就能选对。

句子 “People's understanding of themselves, and their relationship with their environment are all framed in terms of concepts expressed in their own languages,” says Marcus Colchester, director of the Forest Peoples Programme.

Q34

解析 原文提到的“打猎、捕鱼和务农（hunting, fishing and farming）”这些日常活动，在选项中唯一对应的上位归纳词就是“职业/营生（occupations）”。

干扰 你可能在原文找不到原词而卡住，实际上hunting等具象化的动作是在对occupations这个概念进行举例说明，需要学会上下位词转换。

句子 “Many indigenous peoples derive their identities from the way they live off their land. Day-to-day activities such as hunting, fishing and farming are directly connected to the spirits and mythic beings whose stories make these people who they are.”

Q35

解析 原文说明失去语言会丢失知识宝库，而这些知识能为人类问题提供替代“解决方案（solutions）”，这里的solutions同义替换为选项中的“思路/点子（ideas）”。

干扰 顺着原文找solutions可能找不到一模一样的选项，你要灵活把solutions和ideas联系起来，它们在此处都表示“解决问题的方法”。

句子 Louisa Maffi of Terralingua, an organisation that protects cultural and biological diversity, believes linguistic diversity is of immense value to humanity as a whole. As we lose each language, we lose a repository of knowledge, values and beliefs that, in many cases, provide alternative solutions to human problems; we diminish that pool of creativity and inventiveness, and our ability to adapt to changing circumstances.

Q36

解析 第一段通过对比总人数少但小孩在用的Onge语和总人数多但年轻人不用的Chipewyan语，是为了证明“年轻一代是否使用”才是判断一门语言濒危程度的“关键因素（key factor）”。

干扰 你可能选C（语言受威胁的不同原因），但原文并没有分析这两种语言“为什么”受威胁，而是探讨如何“评估”受威胁的程度标准。

句子 However, the total number of speakers is not always a clear indication of the health of a language. In the South Andaman Islands, for example, fewer than 100 people speak Onge, but it is the primary language of those who do, and, critically, the first language of all the islands' children. Consequently, it would be considered less threatened than a language such as Chipewyan in Canada, where more than 4,000 belong to the ethnic group that uses the language, but there is little use among the new generation.

Q37

解析 原文明确指出罗马人促使人类居住在“更大的社区（larger communities）”，而现今人们搬到城市也是一种“城市化”，这对应了选项中“向更广泛的社会群体转变（living in more extended social groups）”这一相似性。

干扰 你可能看到trade就盲目选A，但原文提到罗马时期的trade时，并没有将其用来与“现代（present day）”的情况作类比。

句子 And similar processes are threatening minority languages today, says Ostler. “The Romans succeeded in making people live in larger communities, what we now call urbanisation. And nowadays people move from the countryside to cities where regional languages aren't maintained. The new generation grows up with their lives focused on the wider community.

Q38

解析 原文中“misconceived（错误认识的）”直接对应题干的“wrongly believe”，而这个错误的观念正是“要么保全母语要么学习主流语言的二选一思想（either/or ideology）”，直接对应D选项。

干扰 看到原文说“无法参与国家生活”你可能会误选B，但这是整个“错误二选一观念”里的一个结果，作者抨击的核心在于“被迫二选一（choose between）”这个荒谬的前提。

句子 There is essentially a misconceived either/or ideology: either you maintain your mother tongue, in which case you can't participate in national life, or you forget your mother tongue and learn the majority language.”

Q39

解析 第八段结尾指出，媒体宣传的主流生活方式让年轻人（children）觉得很难去“重视（value）”自己的母语，这正对应A选项中“年轻人对母语的看法/感知（perceptions）”出现了问题。

干扰 你可能选B（代际间的沟通障碍），原文虽然提到年轻人和老人说不同语言，但段落最终点明的问题根源在于“年轻人内心不再认可母语”，而不是单纯没法交流。

句子 The pervasive influence of the media has effectively created a cultural divide between the generations. Ostler continues, where young people speak their traditional language with their elders, but English among themselves. Maffi describes similar trends among indigenous minority groups worldwide. “All of the images children see in the media are of the glamorised lifestyle of the majority, and that lifestyle is communicated in the majority language. So it becomes very difficult for them to find a reason to value their own language.”

Q40

解析 原文指出互联网的好处在于“缺乏控制（lack of control）”以及少数群体可以利用这种“自治权（autonomy）”去记录语言，这与选项B中的“用户的自由（freedom）”完美契合。

干扰 你可能看到原文有video、written等形式就错选A（多样的媒体形式），但这只是表现形式，Peter Austin强调的核心原因是这一切背后的“无人管辖的自由（lack of control / autonomy）”。

句子 Peter Austin, of London's School of Oriental and African Studies, attributes this to the lack of control on the internet. “Unlike most TV or radio, the web isn't in the hands of big media corporations. All you need is an internet account and a little technology, and you can produce information, news, videos, and so on, as much as you want.” Minority groups around the world—in Hawaii, Mexico, Siberia, and many other places—are now taking advantage of this autonomy to document their language in written, audio and visual format.
